# 4. Restorative Functions {#sec-functions}

The two axes — the [scale transect](1-the-scale-transect.qmd) and the [sharing–sparing axis](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd) — and the [archetypes](6-archetypes.qmd) they produce are the document's **structure register**: a coordinate system, mapped by Figure 3. But neither axis is about restoration, and the document is titled *Restorative*. The restorative content is a second register that the structure does not capture: a short vocabulary of restorative **functions** — capacities the land can be made to deliver — that do not sit at a single point on the scale × sharing plane. They are obtainable, to varying degrees, across many structural positions at once.

**A category correction.** Some terms are used as if they named a structural position when they really name a function. *Pollinator habitat* is often treated as position S3, but it is a function reachable at S2 (wildflower interrows over grazing), at S3 (dedicated habitat), and even on a restored S4 parcel. *Native grassland* is the same. Once function and position are separated, the confusion dissolves: positions are **rows**, functions are **columns**, and a real project lights up a *bundle* of function-cells rather than occupying one.

**The relationship is a matrix, not a third axis.** Archetypes (rows) × functions (columns); each cell is the degree to which an archetype makes a function reachable. This is the working-landscapes view — that a mosaic of positions can carry many functions at once rather than trading them off wholesale (Kremen 2015; Grass et al. 2019 — *trace before citing*). A full grid is deferred alongside the Levers × Scale-Zones matrix (§7, open issue 6); the columns are defined here first.

**A palette of capacities, not a scorecard.** These functions are a palette. There is no ranking, and nothing here implies that a good project maximizes every column — most sites can advance only a few, and some functions trade against each other and against generation, capital, and agricultural continuity. Each function's availability is site- and design-conditional, exactly as §2.2 treats the climate-conditionality of full sharing. Naming the functions gives the "restorative" in the title a structural home; it does not prescribe one.

**Scope: biophysical.** The functions below are the biophysical capacities the *land* delivers. The social and economic dimension of restoration — community prosperity, local benefit, and the securing of social license — is real and genuinely co-equal, but it is carried by the [design pressures and levers](3-design-pressures.qmd) (the forces-and-instruments register — [screening](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-screening) and [community benefit](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) live there), not by a land function. In the [SCALE footprint](#sec-scale) below, these biophysical functions are the **Landscapes** domain (with parts of Agriculture); Communities is the social register, and Energy the design pressures.

Each entry is tagged with **(a)** its mechanism, **(b)** its design dependencies — the levers and positions that enable it, **(c)** where on the structural map it is most vs. least available, and **(d)** its evidence status, following the verified / *trace-before-citing* discipline of the [Sources](sources.qmd).

---

### The SCALE footprint {#sec-scale}

A project's influence can be accounted across four domains — **Sustainable Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, and Energy** (SCALE) — a holistic footprint in which each axis runs from regenerative to depleting. The domains line up with this document's own registers: Communities ≈ [social license](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) and [community benefit](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit); **Landscapes** ≈ the restorative functions in this chapter (water, ecosystems); Energy ≈ the [design pressures](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) (cost, security); Agriculture ≈ agricultural continuity and the sharing–sparing axis (food security, marginality). The lexicon borrows SCALE's *domains* as a way to organize influence, but not its evaluative "limit of sustainability" — it names domains, not scores. The name is apt for a document built on the [scale transect](1-the-scale-transect.qmd): what a project regenerates or depletes is itself read at a scale.

![The SCALE footprint: a project's influence accounted across four domains (Sustainable Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, Energy) and their sub-axes, each running from regeneration at the centre to depletion at the rim. The lexicon adopts the domains descriptively; the footprint polygon shown is illustrative, not a score.](../figures/fig5_scale_footprint.svg){#fig-scale}

---

### 4.1 Hydrologic function {#sec-fn-hydrologic}

**Mechanism.** An array reshapes the site water balance. Panels intercept rainfall and redistribute it — concentrating flow along drip lines at panel edges while sheltering the ground beneath — which alters the partition between infiltration, runoff, and evaporation. Shade lowers soil-surface evaporation and plant transpiration, so soil moisture is generally retained; altered cover and compaction change infiltration capacity; and the net effect on deep percolation, groundwater recharge, and stormwater runoff depends on how the ground layer and grading are designed. Restorative hydrologic design uses the array and its ground layer deliberately — to raise infiltration and recharge, to slow and filter runoff (reducing erosion and nutrient export), and to buffer soil moisture through dry spells.

**Design dependencies.** Ground-layer composition is primary — deep-rooted perennial cover infiltrates where bare or gravel ground sheds. Panel and row geometry set where drip concentrates; grading and the placement logic of the [buffer-integrated archetype](6-archetypes.qmd) (siting along hydrologic features) put infiltration where runoff collects; the operational regime and the choice of ground cover carry the rest. The instrument migrates along the transect exactly as the [restoration modes](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) do — siting-led along hydrologic features at A2–A3, management-led through ground cover at A4–A5.

**Where on the map.** Broadly available, because water moves through every site — but most *legible* where the ground layer is designed for it (S2–S4: grazing, prairie/buffer, restored marginal ground) and least so under bare-ground or gravel management. The buffer-integrated archetype is its characteristic siting-led case; managed perennial cover is its characteristic case at scale.

**Evidence status.** The microclimate-to-soil-moisture link is **verified**: panel shade raises soil moisture and cuts evaporative and transpiration losses in drylands [@barrongafford2019], semi-arid grassland arrays show measurable aridity mitigation [@sturchio2025], water is the primary ecological variable in a water-limited framing of ecovoltaics [@knapp2024], and soil-moisture retention is documented in desert array interspaces [@pinos2026]. The *infiltration / recharge / stormwater-runoff* side — how panel drip and altered cover reshape the water balance at depth and at the plot-to-watershed scale — is **thinner and partly trace** (a solar-hydrology review, Yavari et al. 2022, *trace before citing*). This is an active research frontier, and exactly what current field instrumentation is built to close: measured panel drip and runoff, soil-moisture profiles, and coupled surface–groundwater modelling. The honest statement is that the hydrologic function is real, partly evidenced on its microclimate side, and partly a research frontier.

---

### 4.2 Soil & carbon function {#sec-fn-soil}

**Mechanism.** The array changes what the soil is asked to do. Where perennial, low-disturbance cover replaces a tilled row-crop baseline, roots stay in the ground year-round, traffic and tillage fall away, and soil organic carbon and aggregate stability can build back — the standard perennialization pathway, here running under and between the panels. The array's own shade and reduced evaporative demand alter the decomposition and moisture regimes that govern how fast carbon accumulates or turns over. Restorative soil design treats the ground layer as the working surface: perennial establishment, minimal disturbance, and a management regime that keeps cover continuous rather than resetting it. Construction cuts the other way — grading, trenching, and compaction during installation strip and disturb soil, so the early ledger can show a loss before it shows a gain.

**Design dependencies.** Ground-layer composition and establishment method are primary — deep-rooted perennial or native mix under no-till builds where an annual, tilled understory does not. Grazing regime and stocking density set whether animal return of nutrients and trampling help or compact; construction sequencing and traffic-lane discipline decide how much of the starting soil is lost to the build. As with the hydrologic function, the instrument is siting-led early on the transect (which ground is disturbed, and how) and management-led at scale (the ground cover and grazing regime carried over years). The gains are slow and cumulative, so the operational regime — sustained, not one-time — carries most of the outcome.

**Where on the map.** Most reachable under perennial and grazed cover and native-grassland restoration (S2–S3), where the ground layer is designed for continuity, and on restored marginal ground (S4) recovering from a degraded baseline. Least available under annual tillage inside full-sharing cropping (S1) or wherever disturbance is frequent, since each reset spends the accumulated carbon. The grazed-habitat and buffer-integrated archetypes are its characteristic cases; the marginal-land case depends on how degraded the starting soil was.

**Evidence status.** Early soil-carbon and soil-surface gains are **verified** for early-stage ecovoltaic grassland restoration [@krasner2025] — but the same evidence carries the caveats plainly: outcomes are **time-dependent**, the trajectory can start with construction-disturbance losses before it turns positive, and the magnitude is site-conditional on the starting baseline and climate. Longer-term accrual — whether early gains persist and deepen over the array's decades — is **thinner and largely trace**, a frontier rather than a settled number. The honest statement is that the soil function is directionally real and early-evidenced, with the multi-decade curve still open.

### 4.3 Biodiversity & habitat function {#sec-fn-biodiversity}

This entry is the natural home for the category correction above: *pollinator habitat* and *native grassland* are functions reachable across S2–S4, not fixed to S3.

**Mechanism.** Habitat is built from the ground layer up. Floral plantings supply nectar and pollen; the vegetation's vertical and horizontal structure supplies nesting substrate, cover, and the heterogeneity that lets many species partition a single site — so pollinators, ground-nesting arthropods, and grassland birds find resources an annual monoculture does not offer. The array furniture adds its own structure, and the management regime that keeps the planting diverse and undisturbed does as much as the seed mix. Restorative habitat design uses the interrows and array margins as the working habitat, not incidental green space.

**Design dependencies.** Seed-mix composition sets the ceiling — a native, floral-rich mix reaches species a turf understory cannot. Mowing and grazing *timing* is decisive, not merely their presence: disturbance during nesting or bloom undoes the resource it was meant to provide, so the operational calendar is a design lever in its own right. Fragmentation geometry and the [influence-zone](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-footprint-influence) edge matter — several small arrays scattered through a landscape connect and edge differently than a few large ones, and edge-to-area ratio shapes which species the site reaches. As with the other functions, the instrument is siting-led where placement stitches into existing corridors and management-led where the ground cover and its calendar carry the habitat over years.

**Where on the map.** Obtainable across the productive-ecological middle and the spared end (S2–S4) — wildflower interrows over grazing (S2), dedicated habitat plantings (S3), and restored parcels (S4) — which is exactly why it reads as a function reachable at many positions rather than one. Least available under bare-ground, gravel, or intensively disturbed understories. The buffer-integrated and grazed-habitat archetypes are its characteristic cases.

**Evidence status.** **Verified** for grassland-bird gains at solar sites [@walston2025], for insect-community response to habitat establishment [@walston2024], and for bee-species diversity in pollinator-planted arrays [@bruningasocolar2025]. But the finding is **context-dependent**, and the honest reading says so: the marginal habitat benefit is greatest where the surrounding landscape is already sparse in semi-natural habitat, and correspondingly smaller where semi-natural habitat is abundant. It is a real gain, not a uniform good — its size is set by what the site would otherwise have been, not by the planting alone.

### 4.4 Microclimate & thermal–water buffering function {#sec-fn-microclimate}

**Mechanism.** The array rewrites the near-surface energy balance. Panels intercept and redistribute incoming radiation, so daytime soil and canopy temperatures fall in their shade, longwave sheltering raises nighttime minima, and the vapor-pressure deficit under the array drops — the microenvironment swings less far in both directions across the day. That buffering couples tightly to the [hydrologic function](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-hydrologic): the same shade that cuts thermal extremes also cuts evaporative demand, so moisture is retained and the two functions rise and fall together. Restorative microclimate design tunes the geometry so the shelter lands where a heat- or water-stressed ground layer needs it, without starving it of the light it still requires.

**Design dependencies.** Module geometry and mounting height, row spacing and ground-coverage ratio, and tracking schedule set how much radiation is redistributed and where the shade falls through the day. For crops, the shade-tolerance match is decisive — the buffering is a benefit only where the ground layer can trade light for relief, and a cost where it cannot. The effect is inseparable from scale and array geometry: the same panels that shelter a dryland understory can over-shade a light-limited one, which is why this function turns on the design tipping-point rather than existing uniformly. The instrument is geometry-led throughout, and its sign flips with climate and crop.

**Where on the map.** Pronounced in hot, water-limited settings and for shade-tolerant ground layers, where lowered temperature and vapor-pressure deficit relieve real stress; muted to adverse in cool or humid settings and for light-demanding crops, where the shade subtracts more than it buffers. It is itself scale- and geometry-dependent — the [design tipping-point noted in §1.1](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) — so its availability is set by the array's form and the site's climate together, not by position on the sharing–sparing axis alone.

**Evidence status.** **Verified** for the underlying principles and for dryland effects: agrivoltaic and ecovoltaic microclimates redistribute radiation and buffer temperature and moisture [@sturchio2023; @sturchio2025], and soil-moisture and thermal moderation are documented in desert array interspaces [@pinos2026], with the foundational dryland shade-and-moisture link established for arid agrivoltaics [@barrongafford2019]. The crop-facing magnitudes — how much the buffering helps or hurts a given crop — are carried by the shade-tolerance sources in [§5](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics) and remain **climate- and crop-conditional**. The honest statement is that the physics is verified and the dryland benefit is well-evidenced, while the sign and size of the effect in temperate and humid settings depend on a geometry-by-climate match this project treats as conditional.

### 4.5 Archetypes across the domains {#sec-fn-archetypes}

The [archetypes](6-archetypes.qmd) and the functions meet in a matrix: each archetype, by settling its pressures a particular way, produces a characteristic profile across the [SCALE](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-footprint-influence) domains — which of Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, and Energy it foregrounds, and which it trades away. This is the archetype × function matrix read one row at a time; it restates each archetype's *dominant* and *yielded* pressures (§6) in the domain vocabulary, not a new judgment.

![Each archetype's characteristic emphasis across the four SCALE domains, read from its dominant and yielded pressures (§6). Descriptive profiles — what each archetype foregrounds, site-conditional — not a ranking and not a score against a limit of sustainability.](../figures/fig6_archetype_footprints.svg){#fig-archetypes}

- **Overstory Agrivoltaic** (A2 · S1) leans on **Agriculture** (production continues in the footprint) and **Communities** (farmer visibility, local acceptance), trading **Energy** (high clearance and crop-set row spacing cost generation and capital).
- **Grazed Habitat Array** (A4–A5 · S2–S3) foregrounds **Energy** (utility-scale generation) and **Landscapes** (grazed ground cover and habitat), with **Agriculture** present only as a grazing service, not the farm's own operation.
- **Buffer-Integrated Array** (A3 · S3) is a **Landscapes** archetype first — the hydrologic and ecosystem buffer (water, ecosystems) — with **Communities** benefit visible, yielding some **Energy** to buffer geometry.
- **Marginal-Land Diversification** (A2–A3 · S4) is anchored in **Communities** — the farm's financial resilience — using **Agriculture**'s marginal ground, with **Energy** cheap to build but modest in yield.

No archetype fills every domain, and none is meant to: the profiles differ because the pressures were settled differently. A real project's profile is its own, shaped by site and design; these four are reference shapes, not targets. Whether to overlay the SCALE *limit of sustainability* — turning these descriptive profiles into an evaluation of depletion vs. regeneration — is the call the [metrics open issue](7-open-issues.qmd) (§7, issue 5) leaves deliberately unmade.

---

### Associated Terminology

Terms this section introduces; cross-referenced terms link to their home section.

- **Restorative function** — a restorative capacity of the land (hydrologic, soil & carbon, biodiversity & habitat, microclimate) obtainable to varying degrees across many structural positions; a *column* of the archetype × function matrix. Defined here.
- **Function register / structure register** — the two composing registers: structure = the scale × sharing–sparing axes and the [archetypes](6-archetypes.qmd) they produce; function = these restorative capacities that overlay them.
- **Archetype × function matrix** — the descriptive model relating the two registers: archetypes as rows, functions as columns, cells as the degree to which an archetype makes a function reachable. A palette, not a scorecard.
